newsitem.title: USA: Intel chief says future of video games business is PCs.
newsitem.headline: Intel chief says future of video games business is PCs.

text.p: Intel Corp. Chairman Andrew Grove Friday encouraged the video game software industry to consider the personal computer as the most important platform, instead of consoles.
Speaking at the Electronic Entertainment Expo, Grove, who heads the world's biggest maker of PC chips, said the video game industry should shift its focus to the PC while the industry is healthy.
"The definition that we are in the video game business is too restrictive," Grove said. "We need to open it to a definition that says this is a business that sells interactive entertainment."

In a standing room only keynote speech at the video game industry's most influential trade show, Grove showed off the graphics and sound capabilities of the Pentium II, Intel's top- of-the-line microprocessor. The games and computer-animated graphics Grove demonstrated rivaled the quality of state-of-the-art console systems from Nintendo Co. and Sony Corp.
Grove also pointed out that the PC can be used to do things consoles cannot, like edit video, act as a videophone and communicate with others through the Internet.
While shipments of video game consoles are the best they have been in years, developers should consider switching to PCs now while their businesses are strong, Grove said.
Shipments of "home PCs will likely stay ahead of consoles," he said.

The PC traditionally has not been the main venue for video games, mostly because of an average price tag of $1,500. In contrast, console systems from Nintendo, PlayStation and Sega Enterprises Ltd cost less than $150. About 15 million consoles will be shipped in the next 12 months, according to industry estimates.

Most of the new video game titles previewed at the E3 trade show in Atlanta this week are designed to run on console systems. The console is in no danger of being overtaken by the PC any time soon, executives said.
"We've hear this nonsense before," said Howard Lincoln, chairman of Nintendo's North American operation. "PCs were supposed to eat our lunch two years ago and they haven't even taken a bite yet."
